title: Fourteen Years After Acquittal and the Birth of Constitutional Compensation
hook: Kept behind bars for more than fourteen years after a court acquitted him, a former prisoner won the Supreme Court's first constitutional tort damages.

summary: Arrested in 1953, a prisoner in Bihar was acquitted by the Sessions Court at Muzaffarpur in June 1968, yet remained locked behind bars for more than fourteen additional years. An August 30, 1968 jail order kept him detained pending further state instructions, and even a Civil Surgeon's certificate on February 18, 1977 declaring him normal failed to secure his freedom.

He was finally released on October 16, 1982—two days after a Law Department letter—only after a habeas corpus writ petition was filed directly in the Supreme Court under Article 32. When the State tried to justify the fourteen-year delay by alleging unsoundness of mind without producing a single medical record, the court rejected the excuse as a callous cover-up.

On August 1, 1983, a three-judge bench broke new constitutional ground by ruling that Article 21 would be reduced to an empty promise if Article 32 remedies stopped at mere release from illegal detention. Ordering Bihar to pay 30,000 rupees in interim compensation within two weeks without barring a separate civil suit, the judgment established monetary damages for fundamental rights violations.

judgment.outcome: Writ petition allowed with directions; State of Bihar ordered to pay 30,000 rupees in interim compensation within two weeks (in addition to 5,000 rupees already paid), without prejudice to a civil suit for full damages.
points: Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court not only to order release from unlawful detention, but also to award monetary compensation as a palliative for grave violations of Article 21.
Refusing to compensate a citizen robbed of fourteen years of liberty after acquittal would strip the constitutional guarantee of personal liberty of any real meaning.
The State's belated claim of mental illness collapsed because authorities produced no medical records and ignored the Civil Surgeon's 1977 fitness certificate.
An interim writ award does not extinguish the victim's right to file an ordinary civil suit for full damages against the State and erring officials.

principles.name: Monetary Compensation as a Public Law Remedy
principles.meaning: When state officials flagrantly violate fundamental rights under Article 21, constitutional courts may award direct financial compensation under Article 32.
principles.inThisCase: Instead of forcing an impoverished former prisoner to wait decades in civil litigation, the Supreme Court ordered immediate interim relief of 30,000 rupees.

principles.name: Strict Accountability for Post-Acquittal Detention
principles.meaning: Once a court acquits an accused, the State has no legal authority to hold them indefinitely under vague administrative orders.
principles.inThisCase: The court condemned the fourteen-year detention after June 1968 and rejected unsubstantiated claims of insanity.

principles.name: Preservation of Civil Damages Claims
principles.meaning: Interim constitutional compensation acts as immediate relief rather than a ceiling on full tort recovery.
principles.inThisCase: The bench explicitly left the petitioner free to pursue a separate civil suit for complete damages.

takeaways: Constitutional courts can award monetary compensation directly in writ petitions for unlawful detention.
Administrative lethargy or unverified claims of mental illness cannot justify holding an acquitted person in prison.
Interim public-law damages do not bar a victim from seeking full compensation in civil court.

social.hook: Imagine being acquitted by a court, yet kept locked in prison for fourteen more years.
social.script: Imagine being acquitted by a court, yet kept locked in prison for fourteen more years. Arrested in 1953, a prisoner in Bihar was acquitted in June 1968, but an administrative order kept him behind bars. Even after a Civil Surgeon certified him normal in 1977, he stayed jailed until October 1982, when a habeas corpus petition reached the Supreme Court. On August 1, 1983, the court rejected the State's unsupported excuse of mental illness and broke new constitutional ground. It ruled that Article 21 would mean nothing if Article 32 stopped at mere release, ordering 30,000 rupees in interim compensation and birthing constitutional tort damages in India. You be the judge. Full case notes are on the Courtroom Chronicles website.
